newsitem.title: UK: IPE aims to launch European gas futures by Oct 1998.
newsitem.headline: IPE aims to launch European gas futures by Oct 1998.

text.p: The International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) is aiming to launch European natural gas futures contract before October 1998, an IPE official told Reuters on Thursday.
That is the date when the Interconnector, a 20 billion cubic metre a year pipeline from Bacton in eastern England to Zeebrugge in Belgium opens.
"Certainly something needs to be in place before the Interconnector starts," said Stephen Barraclough, Assistant Vice President, Product Development and Research at the IPE.
The IPE will organise the first meeting of a new European Gas Working Group this autumn to coordinate the exchange's planned entry into the European gas market next year, he said.

He said the IPE is already in discussions with interested parties in other European countries to consider the exchange's best way forward for the European market. These include distributors, gas transmission companies, and end users such as fertiliser, steel and glass makers and other large users of gas.

The proposed European working group will bring together players in the Netherlands, Belgium, France and Germany, "places where people are actively involved with the gas directive (now being discussed by the European Union) and who over time will see the benefits of lower prices." It is intended that the group should meet quarterly.
One of the main issues the group must discuss is a possible delivery point.
"Gas is delivered entry paid at the National Balancing Point. We would like to consider if that's appropriate, or if gas at Bacton or Zeebrugge would be more appropriate."

He added that because end users in most European countries have a restricted list of possible suppliers, "there's not much gas purchasing expertise in, say, Holland," and there is a role for the IPE in offering facilities for these companies to buy gas futures and take physical delivery.

The IPE is already taking advice from an existing gas working group which meets quarterly and consists of around 35 companies in the U.K. market, including producers, shippers, futures brokers, traders and the IPE itself.

Barraclough, who recently joined the IPE to develop the natural gas futures contract, said the exchange is also looking at possible changes to the way the contract now operates. They are considering a market making scheme, "raising incentives for one or more active players to make a market." This may be raised at the next meeting of the gas working group, he said.
And he said the contract may move closer to the existing over-the-counter (OTC) spot market.
Users of the contract have said they would like to see contracts for day ahead gas, balance of the current month, and quarters, as well as single months, he said.

The IPE is also looking at offering a within day market, which could compete with the flexibility mechanism for daily gas balancing operated by BG plc pipeline arm Transco as well as with the spot market.

Developing the contract at delivery points other then the NBP still requires a resolution of the problems surrounding Claims Validation, the procedure for confirming that physical delivery has been made. But Barraclough said that this is still some way from being settled.
The existing UK gas futures contract started at the end of January on the IPE and has had mixed fortunes.

Although the opening day saw 465 lots traded, equal to around a fifth of UK daily natural gas production acccording to the exchange, volumes since then have been highly erratic. It is common for whole days or more to pass with no trade done at all.
"I'm not personally disappointed by the level of activity now," said Barraclough.
"Look at Nymex (where natural gas futures is the fastest growing contract), it took a reasonable time to grow."
He added that one reason for the low volume of trade may be that the contract was launched at the end of January, towards the end of the peak winter period rather than at the beginning.
"In hindsight it was not necessarily entirely the right time, but it was still important to go ahead," he said.
--Sebastian Alison, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 6412
